solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: See 26
Surprise details describing long-distance runner

indicators.note: read as de-tails, i.e. remove the tail end, so the final letter of the surprise word goes

parts.note: to surprise is to amaze
describing is 'on', as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: Unexpected particulars emerge in an account of a marathon athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'details' is split as de-tails: AMAZE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The great South American river runs for thousands of miles, a runner in the sense of a flowing river.

clue.text: In confirmation, old Don's very, very tired

indicators.note: the donning word is placed in the confirming word, which surrounds it

parts.note: AY is an old form of aye, a word of confirmation
to don clothes is to wear them

explanation.surface: An elderly university don, when asked, confirms he is utterly exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a university teacher but is the verb to put on.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an archaic and poetic word for worn out or weary.

clue.text: Time behind bars, maybe, following round to be paid for later

indicators.note: the prison-and-time part follows, so comes after, the round letter

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O

indicators.note: time is put behind bars, i.e. locked inside the prison word

parts.note: behind bars suggests prison, slang NICK

explanation.surface: A prison sentence after a round of drinks, settled later.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying on credit, with payment deferred, is an idiom for goods bought without paying now.

clue.text: 'I don't belieeeeve it!' — funny: this is Victor, remember!

indicators.note: funny in the sense of odd or peculiar tells us to rearrange the letters that follow

parts.note: Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Victor Meldrew's catchphrase, from the British sitcom One Foot in the Grave, is recalled as a comic one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I don't belieeeeve it!' is the catchphrase of grumpy Victor Meldrew in the British sitcom One Foot in the Grave, so 'Victor' looks like part of the scene but just gives V.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of astonishment, the pirate's oath standing for the sitcom's cry of disbelief.

clue.text: Time Magazine? Not the current one

definitions.text: Time Magazine? Not the current one

parts.words: Time Magazine? Not the current one
parts.note: a magazine from a past time, not this week's edition, is an earlier number of the publication

explanation.surface: Someone asks for the famous US news weekly, but an old edition rather than this week's.
explanation.walkthrough: Time Magazine looks like the American title, but read it as a magazine from an earlier time.
explanation.definitionFit: An earlier edition of a periodical, no longer on sale as the latest, is called this.

clue.text: Bliss in saying grace? In desecrated houses that is not so

indicators.note: the rearranged letters house, or hold inside them, the denial
desecrated means violated or spoiled, so the letters of grace and in are disordered

parts.note: a flat denial, that is not so, is NO

explanation.surface: Is it blissful to say grace in churches that have been desecrated? No.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'ignorance is bliss' supplies the definition: bliss, in the saying, is this.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb equates lack of knowledge with happiness, so in that saying bliss stands for it.

clue.text: Together these presenters might be seen to be mother

definitions.text: Together these presenters might be seen to be mother

parts.words: Together these presenters might be seen to be mother
parts.note: the two short names of a British TV duo, joined in the other order, make a word meaning pour out, and to be mother is to pour the tea

explanation.surface: A famous pair of TV hosts seem, together, to take on a maternal role.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant and Dec are a British TV presenting duo; 'be mother' is British for pouring the tea, i.e. DECANT, which is DEC + ANT.
explanation.definitionFit: The duo's names combined give a verb for pouring, the British idiom for serving the tea.

clue.text: Totally valid rant

definitions.meaning: to go on and on loudly about something, as a verb phrase

explanation.surface: A tirade that is entirely justified.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for exactly right, and also a phrasal verb for haranguing at length.

clue.text: Fine Royal Burgh's seen through the agony

indicators.note: the burgh is seen through, i.e. right inside, the agony word

parts.note: agony is pain
Perth is a Scottish town with royal burgh status

explanation.surface: A splendid Scottish town is endured through suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like praise but means very thin. A royal burgh is a Scottish town granted a royal charter; Perth is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine as in delicate or slender, the hyphenated adjective describing something extremely slight.

clue.text: Ian must ring Ken in the morning — time Dr John Friend could assist …

indicators.note: the name Ian is made to ring, i.e. surround, the following letters

parts.note: taken as written, a man's name
to ken is Scots for to know
AM, ante meridiem, means in the morning
the Time Lord doctor of the TV series is Doctor Who
john is slang for a toilet, as is can

explanation.surface: Ian is to phone Ken first thing, when a Dr John Friend may be able to help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ken' looks like a second name but is the Scots verb; 'John' gives CAN, slang for a lavatory, and the Doctor is the Time Lord of Doctor Who.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock assurance that a contact or acquaintance has the skills to help out.

clue.text: See 13
… and it's me admitting error!

parts.note: following on from the previous clue, the speaker concedes a mistake with a stock phrase

explanation.surface: The ellipsis continues the previous clue: the setter owns up to a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the set formula someone says to concede they were wrong once shown the truth.

clue.text: Escalating ego displayed in crossword pattern — is setter in a form of control?

indicators.note: in a down entry, escalating means climbing upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top
the ego is displayed within the pattern word, sitting inside it

parts.note: the pattern of black and white squares is the grid
the ego is the self, I
the setter refers to himself as ME

explanation.surface: A crossword setter wonders whether showing off his ego in the grid amounts to controlling solvers.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived term names state direction and control of the economy.

clue.text: See 11
Steps through church so described with enmity

indicators.note: the steps pass through the church word, landing in its middle

parts.note: the church is commonly described as holy, as in Holy Church
a stile is a set of steps over a fence

explanation.surface: Someone climbs steps through a churchyard in a spirit of animosity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steps' gives STILE, steps for climbing over a fence or wall, common on British country footpaths.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with enmity means acting in an unfriendly, antagonistic manner.

clue.text: Current 27 confirmed as President

parts.note: 27 is 'Me myself I', so the self confirmed in post would say I am, giving AM

explanation.surface: The present incumbent, referenced by another clue, is confirmed in office as President.
explanation.walkthrough: On being confirmed, 27 (I) would say 'I am P(resident)'; drop the I already given by 27 and AM + P remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrical current is measured in units named after Ampère, abbreviated to these letters.

clue.text: Using the byline in breakaway

indicators.note: the letters sit in the word breakaway, inside it

explanation.surface: A journalist writes under a byline in a breakaway publication.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation for also known as introduces an alias, such as a pen name used on a byline.

clue.text: Poet Laureate it's easy to discuss

indicators.note: when you discuss something you speak of it, so the word is said out loud

parts.note: the phrase as easy as pie means very easy

explanation.surface: A national poet is a straightforward subject for conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry James Pye was Poet Laureate from 1790 to 1813; 'easy as pie' gives the word spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James Pye held the official royal poet's post in Britain under George III.

clue.text: Melodious religious figure fashioning new clues well!

parts.note: an imam is a Muslim prayer leader
melodious singing is in tune, on key

indicators.note: fashioning means shaping or making, so the letters are reworked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A tuneful cleric composes fresh crossword clues, and does it well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well!' is the exclamation of surprise, not the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of amazement, the colloquial phrase being a jokey way of expressing surprise.

clue.text: Took in mischievous female

definitions.meaning: The Greek goddess of mischief and ruin

explanation.surface: A naughty woman deceived someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took in' looks like deceived but means consumed.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of eat, and the name of the Greek goddess of folly and mischief.

clue.text: Liked by Caledonian inside

definitions.meaning: in favour with someone, on good terms

explanation.surface: A Scot indoors is popular.
explanation.walkthrough: Caledonian means Scottish: the Scots use this word for within.
explanation.definitionFit: Being popular with someone, and a Scottish preposition meaning within.

clue.text: One's pay minus a cut over unpleasant growths

indicators.note: in a down entry, over says the whole string is turned upside down

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: minus says the named letter is subtracted from pay

parts.note: to lop is to cut

explanation.surface: Someone's wages, with a deduction, cause nasty lumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses IPYLOP (I + PY + LOP) to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: These are small tumours or growths protruding from mucous membranes, plural of the singular form.

clue.text: 'Viz' lover upset by Terry's death

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the lover word reads upwards

parts.note: leman is an archaic word for a lover or sweetheart

indicators.note: the death of Terry is its very end, its last letter

explanation.surface: A reader of the British comic magazine Viz is upset by a man called Terry dying.
explanation.walkthrough: Viz is a British adult comic; here it is the abbreviation viz, that is to say. 'upset' turns LEMAN to NAMEL.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation viz (videlicet) introduces a specification, meaning that is to say.

clue.text: I very much approve closure of Parisian compound

parts.note: the Spanish cry ole expresses enthusiastic approval
a Parisian's word for the end or close is fin

explanation.surface: Someone heartily endorses the shutting of a French business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closure' looks like the last letter of Parisian, but it is the French word for end.
explanation.definitionFit: Another name for an alkene, a hydrocarbon chemical compound with a double bond.

clue.text: How The Rake made Progress not very far from the mouth?

parts.note: one millimetre, written 1MM, is not very far, with I as the one
something spoken or taken from the mouth is done orally

explanation.surface: A question about how Hogarth's rake advanced, only a short way from his mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: A Rake's Progress is Hogarth's series of paintings of a young man's dissolute decline.
explanation.definitionFit: The rake progressed through vice and debauchery, that is in a wicked, unprincipled way.

clue.text: Claim of one potentially insatiable Lothario — seduce a libertine!

indicators.note: a libertine is unrestrained and free of rules, so the preceding letters are let loose into a new order

explanation.surface: A seducer's appetite seems endless as he urges a rake to seduce someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of LOTHARIO, SEDUCE and A, rearranged as signalled by 'libertine', give the whole fifteen-letter phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ravenous enough to be insatiable might announce this stock exaggeration of extreme hunger.

clue.text: Song from Grammy-nominated singer recovered from Emmy files

indicators.note: recovered read as re-covered, i.e. given a new arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A track by an award-nominated performer is retrieved from television award files.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is by Joan Armatrading, a Grammy-nominated singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan Armatrading's 1980 hit single carries this title.

clue.text: Firm screening drug in a tight way

indicators.note: the firm word screens, i.e. hides inside it, the drug

parts.note: firm and resolute means manly
E is short for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A company conceals drugs in a stingy fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company but is the adjective; 'tight' means stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is slang for stingy, and acting stingily is acting in a miserly, ungenerous manner.

clue.text: Setting reverses such anagrams signify

indicators.note: reverses applied to the next word says its letters run backwards

parts.note: such, as in 'and so on', is so

indicators.note: anagrams applied to the word signify says its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A setter's instructions name the devices he uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting as in hardening into bone or becoming rigid, like plaster or opinions do.
